TOPIC 1: MITOSIS

What we used to think:
What we now know:
Life can arise from non-living things (abiogenesis)
Life arises only from the division of living cells (biogenesis)

From the moment of fertilization, cells are continuously growing, dying, and being replaced…
… this is achieved through the process of cell division. But before we get into too many details, we have some background info to talk about..

Each new cell, or daughter cell, must contain the same genetic information as the original cell, or parent cell 
DNA is this genetic information. It is found within the nucleus of each and every cell in the body.
parent cell:
Creating identical daughter cells is accomplished through the processes of DNA replication and cell division.

The best way to visualize chromosomes is a karyotype, which is an image of all the chromosomes the nucleus. 
The somatic cells (body cells, ie. not gametes) of humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes or 46 chromosomes in total.
In females, there are 23 pairs of homologous chromosomes (22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of X sex chromosomes) 
In males, there 22 pairs are homologous chromosomes (autosomes), and 1 pair of non-homologous sex chromosomes (“sex chromosomes”)
Homologous chromosomes are chromosomes with the same gene sequence as one another; one homologue is of maternal origin, and the other is of paternal origin.
Although homologues carry the same set of genes, they may carry different forms of the each gene (a.k.a alleles)
Because human cells carry to pairs of each chromosome, we are said to be diploid

Why is the Y-chromosome smaller?
The Y chromosome is smaller because it has lost many genes over time. It started as a pair with the X chromosome, but over millions of years, it stopped recombining with the X and many of its genes degraded. Now, it mainly carries a few genes essential for male traits, like the SRY gene for sex determination.

“Unpackaged” DNA is referred to as chromatin:
DNA exists as chromatin during most of the cell’s life but condenses into chromosomes when the cell is about to divide.
Chromosomes contain very tightly wound DNA.

Before cell division, it is important for chromatin to condense into chromosomes in order to be able to separate them without damage and breakage. Image how hard it would be to separate cooked spaghetti that is all entangled!

Chromosome Number
varies from species to species…





More chromosomes DOES NOT necessarily result in higher intelligence or complexity

Humans = 46
Ferns = 1260
Dogs = 78
Bananas = 22

Human somatic (body) cells are diploid, or “2n”
This means there are two copies of each chromosome (one of maternal origin and one of paternal origin)
Human gametes are haploid, or “n”







2n = 46
n = 23

Some organisms, such as earthworms, contain more than two homologous chromosomes in each cell. These organisms are said to be polyploid. 

Ploidy
Ploidy refers to the number of sets of chromosomes in a cell.

Duplicated Chromosomes
During the S-phase of interphase, DNA is replicated to double the genetic content of the cell. This is to ensure each daughter cell received a copy of each chromosome and the genes on it.  
We can observe this best when looking at unduplicated and duplicated chromosomes.
The two arms of a duplicated chromosome are called sister chromatids and are exact copies of one another (result of S-phase)
Sister chromatids are held together by the centromere

The Cell Cycle
M-phase accounts for the actual division of genetic information (mitosis) and splitting of the cytoplasm itself (cytokinesis)

If you were to look at a sample of healthy tissues under a microscope, most of the cells you would observe would likely be in interphase/early prophase. Why do you think that is?
If cells spend most of their time (approx 90%) in interphase, the chance of finding a particular cell in interphase is much greater. Therefore most cells should be found in interphase at any time of observation. 

Actively growing tissues, such as the the tip of plant roots, however will have a slightly higher proportion of cells in mitosis

What would happen if cells were constantly dividing in an uncontrolled fashion?
CANCER

Cancer & the Cell Cycle
Uncontrolled cell division may be caused by exposure to mutagens, or agents which change an organism’s genetic material. 
Mutagens may be physical, chemical, or biological in origin.
Mutagens that specifically lead to the formation of cancerous cells are further classified as carcinogens.

Mitosis
The extent of repair varies from organism to organism
Is a form of cell division that produces daughter cells that are identical to parent cells.
Mitosis & Growth

Mitosis
After DNA replication (interphase), cells go through four stages of mitosis before cytokinesis can occur:
PMAT! (Your dog peed on the mat..)

Key events:
Chromatin condenses to form chromosomes
Nuclear membrane breaks down
Centrioles move to opposite poles of the cell and spindle fibres begin to form (spindle fibres are required to eventually pull the duplicated chromosomes apart)
At this stage, each pair of homologous chromosomes has already been duplicated, so the cell contains twice as much DNA than normal.
1. PROPHASE
NOTE: These examples only show 4 chromosomes (2n=4), but remember that a actual human cell would be showing 46 chromosomes (2n=46)

2. METAPHASE 
Key events:
Spindle fibres attach to the centromere of each chromosome, guiding them to the equator (middle line) of the cell
Duplicated chromosomes line up in single file, forming the “metaphase plate”

M for middle!

3. ANAPHASE
Key events:
Spindle fibres shorten and sister chromatids are pulled apart from one another; centromeres split
Two opposing poles are formed, each with a complete diploid set of DNA
3. ANAPHASE

4. TELOPHASE
Key events:
Chromosomes reach opposite poles of the cell
Spindle fibres break down
Chromosomes begin to unwind into chromatin
Nuclear membrane forms around each new set of genetic info.

Cytokinesis
Cytoplasm, containing organelles, splits to form two identical daughter cells with the same genetic content as the original parent cell
Daughter cells are now in G1 of interphase

Telophase and cytokinesis in plant cells looks a bit different…
Because plant cells contain a rigid cell wall, cytoplasm will not furrow and pinch off
Instead, a cell plate forms between the two daughter nuclei, eventually developing into a cell wall

Extra: Mitosis and Aging
Telomeres are caps found at the end of each chromosome. Every time a cell divides, its telomeres shorten.
Eventually, the telomeres become so short that a cell will no longer be able to undergo mitosis, and cell death occurs. 
Telomere length thus serves as a sort of “molecular clock” for cellular aging. 
Lifestyle factors such as smoking, lack of physical activity, obesity, stress, exposure to pollution, etc. can potentially increase the rate of telomere shortening, cancer risk, and pace of aging.

https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn3393-dolly-the-sheep-dies-young/

TOPIC 2: MEIOSIS

While somatic (body) cells must contain a complete set of chromosomes, gametes possess just half the genetic information of parent cells. 
This is accomplished through the process of  meiosis.

 
In humans, haploid gametes join during fertilization to form a diploid zygote. 
Meiosis

Meiosis
The outcome of meiosis is different than that of mitosis in three ways:
Produces four non-identical daughter cells rather than two identical ones
Daughter cells have half the chromosomes of parent cells
Daughter cells have chromosomes with different combinations of genes compared to those in parent cells
This is achieved through crossing over (more on this later)

Meiosis
Involves the same stages of cell division as mitosis; however, in meiosis, each stage occurs twice.

Like in mitosis, meiosis begins with interphase, or DNA replication. Entering prophase I, then, the cell contains two pairs of homologous chromosomes.

Key events:
Chromatin condenses to form chromosomes, spindle fibres form, nuclear membrane dissolves, etc. 
Homologous chromosomes pair up and align vertically (called synapsis) and crossing over occurs
PROPHASE I

Crossing over is an opportunity to mix genes.
This increases genetic variation and diversity which is important for sexually reproducing organisms
Recall that homologous chromosomes are a set of the same chromosome, where one is maternal and one is paternal origin. These contain the same genes, but may be different alleles, or versions of those genes, such as the allele for ‘blue eyes’ vs ‘brown eyes’

Two homologous chromosomes aligned during synapsis is called a tetrad. Each tetrad contains 2 sets of 2 sister chromatids (total of 4 chromatids)
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids (there would be no point to cross over between sister chromatids as they are exact replicas of one another)

tetrad

METAPHASE I
Key events:
Spindle fibres attach to the centromere of each chromosome
Instead of lining up in single file as they do in mitosis, chromosomes line up as homologous pairs, so that chromosomes of maternal and paternal origin will end up at opposing poles 
The orientation of each pair of homologous chromosomes is independent of the orientation of the other pairs (independent assortment)

Independent Assortment
(more on this in Chapter 17 as well)
Increases gamete diversity due to number of potential chromosome combinations

Independent Assortment
The following diagram shows the possible gametes that can be formed from a 2n=4 cell due to independent assortment. 
Now imagine the number of possibilities for a human 2n=46 cell! 
To be precise, it would be 223=8388608 possibilities! AND this is just one gamete (sperm or egg) that can join with a completely random gamete with the same 8388608 possibilities! That would be 8388608 x 8388608 = 7036874418000 ways to make a zygote between two parents. AND we haven’t even considered crossing over!!

ANAPHASE I
Key events:
Spindle fibres shorten, pulling homologous chromosomes apart
Sister chromatids remain together, so that each new pole has a full set of DNA
Important:
Anaphase I of Meiosis I is the reduction step. This means that the daughter cells that are produced after Anaphase I are haploid, meaning they only have one copy of each chromosome (i.e. n=23 in humans)

TELOPHASE I (and cytokinesis)
Key events:
Homologous chromosomes begin to uncoil, spindle fibres disappear
Cytoplasm is divided and a nuclear membrane forms around each new set of chromosomes
Each new cell is haploid because they contain either the maternal or paternal set of homologous chromosomes (reduction division has occurred)

MEIOSIS II
Interphase does NOT occur before the cells enter prophase II (i.e. DNA is not replicated)
Meiosis II is a lot like mitosis, with the exception of a haploid cell undergoing division to create identical daughter cells
Cells proceed through prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, and telophase II 
The result is four haploid daughter cells with a single copy of each chromosome

Each daughter cell formed after telophase II will proceed through cytokinesis again to form the final gametes…
In males, this process is referred to as spermatogenesis, and results in the formation of four viable sperm cells

Reduction Division

Why does female gametogenesis involve unequal division of the cytoplasm? I.e. why are polar bodies made without any cytoplasm?
This ensures that the single released ovum contains the maximum amount of cytoplasm including the organelles and nutrients. This will ensure that the developing morula and blastocyst has the means to survive until implantation occurs approx. 7 days after fertilization
Meiosis Recap

Nondisjunction:
When things go wrong
Nondisjunction occurs when chromosomes do not separate properly during meiosis I or meiosis II
Nondisjunction during meiosis I and meiosis II have different outcomes; however, both produce gametes with either too few or too many chromosomes:
trisomy results from having an extra chromosome while
monosomy results from having one less chromosome
Note: Trisomy and monosomy are not the same as being triploid or haploid. In triploid organisms there is an extra copy of every chromosome, whereas in trisomy there is an extra copy of one chromosome. Same situation for haploid vs. monosomy. 
You should be able to determine of disjunction occurred during meiosis I or II from similar diagrams

Incidence of Down Syndrome with maternal age:


As a woman ages, her probability of producing eggs with an extra copy of chromosome 21 increases dramatically. This is thought to happen because centromeres become “sticky” with age, meaning that nondisjunction will occur more readily
Trisomy 21 can also be caused by nondisjunction in sperm cells

Applications of the Cell Cycle: Cloning
Cloning is the process of forming identical offspring from a single cell or tissue of a parent organ. 
Cloning is a form of axexual reproduction. Many species utilize this form of reproduction (e.g. plants, bacteria, hydra)
A form of cloning also results in the production of twins; if a single fertilized egg accidentally undergoes mitosis and splits in two, identical (maternal) or monozygotic twins occur, each with the exact same DNA. 
Non-identical (fraternal) or dizygotic twins form when two eggs are ovulated at once, and are fertilized by different sperm. Dizygotic twins do not share the same genetic information.

TOPIC 3: 
Reproductive Strategies

Reproductive Strategies
The human life cycle relies on regular patterns of meiosis and mitosis. However, other organisms rely on alternative reproductive strategies…
Asexual reproduction: Reproductive process where a parent organism produces genetically identical offspring, typical using mitosis or a similar process.
Sexual reproduction: Involves the production of gametes through meiosis, followed by fertilization between genetically distinct parental gametes to produce genetically distinct offspring.

Binary Fission
Method of reproduction utilized by bacteria
Allows for rapid growth of identical populations through asexual reproduction
Advantages? Disadvantages?
Note: Over the rest of these slides you will be introduced to various reproductive strategies. You will not need to memorize and describe the various strategies. However, you will be expected to identify given a context whether it is sexual or asexual reproduction, where various events take place (mitosis/meiosis/fertilization) and the ploidy at each stage given context.

Conjugation
Also utilized by bacteria
Plasmids (another source of DNA) are transferred from one cell to another through pili
Creates cells with new genetic combinations (kind of like sexual reproduction)

Budding
A form of asexual reproduction in which a complete but miniature version of the parent grows out from the parent’s body; the newly formed clone separates only once it matures
Commonly utilized by metazoans such as corals, sponges, and hydra

Vegetative Reproduction
A form of budding that takes place in plants (asexual reproduction)

Parthenogenesis
A form of asexual reproduction in which an unfertilized egg develops into an adult
Example: Honeybees
The queen bee lays both fertilized and unfertilized eggs
Fertilized eggs develop into female worker bees, while unfertilized eggs develop into male drones

Spores
Form of asexual reproduction which allows parents to disperse their offspring over long distances
Often dispersed by wind or water
May be haploid or diploid
Some spores are actually the product of sexual reproduction (meiosis rather than mitosis), resulting in an alternation of generations

“ALTERNATION OF GENERATIONS”
The life cycle of some plants consists of two generations…
A diploid generation, or sporophyte
A haploid generation, or gametophyte

Through meiosis, the sporophyte (or spore-making body) produces multiple haploid spores, which spread and develop without fertilization. Each spore grows into a plant body called the gametophyte (or gamete-making body), which produces male and female gametes. Upon fertilization, gametes develop into another sporophyte, and the cycle repeats.
General model for alternation of generations:

Many plants spend the majority of their lives in one phase or the other…
Conifers, for example, spend most of their lives in the diploid generation. The tree itself is this diploid sporophyte, while the cones contain the haploid gametophytes.

Rather than alternating between haploid and diploid generations, some organisms simply alternate between sexual and asexual reproduction (e.g. cnidarians):
